title: Mind-Bending Maths · Episode 1
chapters: The doomsday rule: find the weekday of any date in your head
The Monty Hall problem: the puzzle that fools almost everyone
The pigeonhole principle: the simplest idea that proves surprising things

units.t: Mind-Bending Maths. Episode one.

In this episode: The power of doubling, The doomsday rule: find the weekday of any date in your head, The Monty Hall problem: the puzzle that fools almost everyone and The pigeonhole principle: the simplest idea that proves surprising things.
Part one. The power of doubling.
Fold a sheet of paper 42 times and, in theory, it would reach past the Moon.
Doubling is the simplest pattern in maths, and the one our brains are worst at imagining.
The chessboard legend.
An old legend says the inventor of chess was offered any reward by a delighted ruler.
He asked for something that sounded modest: one grain of wheat on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time across all 64 squares.
The ruler laughed and agreed.
He should not have.
By square 11 the pile holds 1,024 grains, still only a handful.
By square 21 it passes a million.
The final square alone needs about 9.
2 quintillion grains, and the whole board adds up to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains, which is 2 multiplied by itself 64 times, minus one.
The world would need many centuries of harvests to grow that much.
Paper to the Moon.
Take a sheet of paper about 0.
1 millimetres thick.
Each fold doubles it.
After 20 folds, if that were possible, it would be about 105 metres tall.
After 30 folds it would pass 100 kilometres, reaching the edge of space.
After 42 folds it would stand about 440,000 kilometres high, past the Moon's average distance of about 384,000.
In reality each fold needs far more paper.
In 2002 the American student Britney Gallivan folded a very long strip 12 times, a record.
Our intuition is built for adding.
Thirty steps of one metre cover 30 metres.
Thirty steps doubling in length would total over a million kilometres, nearly 27 times around the Earth.
Researchers call this 'exponential growth bias'.
Late warnings, quick sums.
A lily patch doubles in area every day and covers the pond on day 48.
On what day was it half covered?
Many say day 24, but it is day 47.
Four days before the end, only about 6 per cent is covered.
Early on the numbers look tiny, and by the time the problem is obvious, few doublings remain.
That is why acting a few days sooner matters so much early in an outbreak.
To estimate doubling time, divide 72 by the yearly percentage growth.
At 6 per cent, it takes about 12 years.
Credit card debt charging 20 per cent would double in under four years if unpaid.
This is general information, not financial advice; moneysmart.
gov.
au has free calculators.
Halving, in reverse.
Doubling has a mirror image: repeated halving.
Radioactive carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years: in that time, half of any sample decays into nitrogen.
After another 5,730 years, half of what is left has gone, leaving a quarter.
After ten half-lives, about 57,000 years, less than a thousandth of the original remains.
Living things constantly take in carbon, so their carbon-14 level stays steady while they are alive.
When they die the clock starts ticking, and by measuring how much is left, scientists can date bones, wood and charcoal back to roughly 50,000 years.
Halving also explains why the amount of a medicine in your blood fades in steps rather than all at once.
Nothing doubles forever.
If a single bacterium dividing every 20 minutes kept going unchecked, its descendants would outweigh the entire Earth in about two days.
That never happens, because food runs out, waste builds up and space fills.
Real growth usually follows an S-shaped curve: slow at first, then explosive, then levelling off.
Mathematicians call this logistic growth.
Technology shows the same pattern.
In 1965 the engineer Gordon Moore noticed that the number of components on a chip was doubling regularly, and in 1975 he revised this to roughly every two years.
Moore's law powered the computer revolution, though progress has slowed as parts approach the size of atoms.
The lesson is to spot doubling early, and to ask what limit will eventually stop it.
The key idea: Doubling one grain across 64 squares produces more wheat than the world could grow in centuries.
Part two. The doomsday rule: find the weekday of any date in your head.
A mathematician named John Conway could tell you the day of the week for any modern date in a couple of seconds.
His method is easy to learn, and it starts with 4 April.
A grim party trick.
In the early 1970s the British mathematician John Horton Conway, famous for inventing the Game of Life, devised a way to work out the weekday of any date mentally.
He built on an earlier method by Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, who was also a mathematician.
The trick rests on a striking fact.
In any given year, a whole collection of memorable dates always land on the same weekday.
Conway called that weekday the year's ‘doomsday’.
The name is not sinister.
It simply means the anchor day for that year.
The anchor dates.
The even months are easy: 4 April, 6 June, 8 August, 10 October and 12 December, 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10, 12/12.
For the odd months, the mnemonic ‘I work 9 to 5 at 7-Eleven’ gives 9 May, 5 September, 11 July and 7 November.
The last day of February is always a doomsday, as is 14 March.
For January, use 3 January in ordinary years and 4 January in leap years.
In 2026 all of these are Saturdays.
Christmas?
The nearest anchor is 12 December, a Saturday, so 19 and 26 December are too, making Christmas a Friday.
Australia Day: 3 January is Saturday, so 31 January is too, making 26 January a Monday.
Moving from year to year.
A normal year has 365 days, which is 52 weeks and one day, so the doomsday moves forward by one weekday.
A leap year adds a day, so the jump after 29 February is two.
In 2026 the doomsday is Saturday.
In 2027 it is Sunday.
In 2028, a leap year, it jumps two places to Tuesday.
To handle any year in a century, start from a known anchor: Wednesday for the 1900s and Tuesday for the 2000s.
Add the number of years past the century, plus the number of leap years in that stretch, and count forward that many weekdays, ignoring complete weeks.
A worked example.
Test the method on Neil Armstrong's Moon step on 20 July 1969, by American time.
The 1900s anchor is Wednesday.
The year is 69 years into the century, which includes 17 leap years, since 69 divided by 4 is 17 with some left over.
Add them: 69 plus 17 is 86.
Remove complete weeks: 86 divided by 7 is 12 weeks with 2 left over.
Two days on from Wednesday makes 1969's doomsday a Friday.
The July anchor is 11 July, a Friday, and so is 18 July.
That makes 20 July a Sunday.
In eastern Australia it was already the next day, so viewers here watched on Monday 21 July.
Why it works.
The method works because the calendar follows fixed rules.
Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582.
A year is a leap year if divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400.
So 1900 was not a leap year but 2000 was.
The 400-year cycle holds 146,097 days, exactly 20,871 weeks, so the calendar repeats perfectly, and the 13th falls on a Friday slightly more often than any other weekday.
Conway reportedly had his computer quiz him with random dates when he logged in.
He died in April 2020.
To learn the method, start with the current year's anchors.
It teaches modular arithmetic: weekdays cycle every seven, as hours cycle every twelve.
The key idea: In any year, a set of memorable dates share one weekday, called the doomsday, which anchors every other date.
Part three. The Monty Hall problem: the puzzle that fools almost everyone.
Three doors, one car, two goats.
Should you switch?
The right answer is simple to state, hard to believe, and once had people with maths doctorates writing angry letters.
Why switching wins.
Imagine a game show with three closed doors: a car behind one, goats behind two.
You pick door 1.
The host, who knows where the car is, always opens another door to reveal a goat, say door 3, and offers a switch to door 2.
Most people feel it is 50 to 50.
The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, host of the American show Let's Make a Deal, and the statistician Steve Selvin posed it in 1975.
Your first pick is the car one time in three.
Then switching loses.
Two times in three you picked a goat, and the host must open the only other goat door, so the last door hides the car.
Switching wins two thirds of the time.
The letters that poured in.
In 1990 a reader sent the puzzle to Marilyn vos Savant, who wrote the 'Ask Marilyn' column in Parade, a US magazine read by millions.
She replied that you should switch, because switching wins two thirds of the time.
The reaction was extraordinary.
She received thousands of letters, many from people with doctorates, many telling her she had made an embarrassing mistake.
She was right.
The puzzle even troubled Paul Erdős, one of the most prolific mathematicians of the twentieth century.
According to a well-known account, he refused to accept the answer until he was shown a computer simulation of the game played many times over.
Expertise does not protect anyone from a strong but faulty intuition.
A hundred doors.
If the answer still feels wrong, imagine 100 doors, with a car behind one and goats behind the other 99.
You pick door 37.
Your chance of being right is just 1 in 100.
Now the host, who knows where the car is, opens 98 of the other doors, every one revealing a goat, and leaves just one other door closed: door 74.
Would you stick with door 37 or switch to door 74?
Almost everyone now feels the pull to switch, and they are right.
Your door still has its original 1 in 100 chance.
The host has carefully avoided the car while opening 98 doors, so door 74 carries the remaining 99 in 100.
The three-door game works the same way, with smaller numbers.
It depends on the host.
There is a subtle condition hidden in the puzzle.
The host knows where the car is, always opens a goat door and always offers the swap.
Change those rules and the answer changes.
Suppose the host has no idea where the car is and opens one of the other two doors at random.
Sometimes he will reveal the car and spoil the game.
But in the games where he happens to reveal a goat, your chances really are 50 to 50, and switching makes no difference.
The difference is information.
A knowing host's choice is limited by where the car is, so his action tells you something useful.
A random host's choice tells you nothing extra.
Many heated arguments about the puzzle are really about which rules apply.
Taming your intuition.
More than 70 years before the game show, the French mathematician Joseph Bertrand described a similar trap in an 1889 book.
One box holds two gold coins, one two silver and one a gold and a silver.
You pick a box at random and draw a gold coin.
Is the other coin gold?
Most say one half, but it is two thirds.
Three gold coins could have been drawn, and two of them sit in the gold box.
Intuition counts the options left and assumes they are equally likely.
Instead, list every equally likely starting situation and follow each through.
Or experiment: play 30 rounds of Monty Hall with cups and a friend as host, always sticking, then 30 always switching.
Switching will usually come out well ahead.
The key idea: Your first pick is right only a third of the time, so switching wins two-thirds of the time.
Part four. The pigeonhole principle: the simplest idea that proves surprising things.
If you have more pigeons than holes, some hole holds two pigeons.
That is the whole idea, and it can prove that two people in Sydney have exactly the same number of hairs.
Too many pigeons.
Ten pigeons fly home to nine pigeonholes.
However they arrange themselves, at least one hole must hold two birds.
There is no trick, no probability and no calculation.
It cannot be otherwise.
This is the pigeonhole principle, perhaps the most obvious statement in all of mathematics.
Mathematicians love it because it proves something must exist without ever finding it.
You need not know which hole is crowded, only that one is.
Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet used the idea in the 1830s and 1840s, and in German it became the Schubfachprinzip, the drawer principle.
The English name probably refers to small desk or mail-sorter compartments, not actual birds.
Socks, birthdays and hair.
Black and grey socks sit jumbled in a dark drawer.
How many must you grab to be certain of a pair?
Three.
Two socks might be one of each, but a third must match one.
The colours are the holes and the socks are the pigeons.
Likewise, among 367 people two must share a birthday, since there are only 366 dates.
Certainty differs from likelihood: a shared birthday is likely with 23 people, but only 367 guarantees it.
Sydney has over five million people.
A head holds roughly 100,000 hairs, perhaps up to 150,000, and nobody has a million.
Make a hole for every count from zero to one million, and at least two Sydneysiders must have exactly the same number.
In fact at least five share one.
When boxes overflow.
A stronger version tells you how crowded a box must be.
Suppose 100 people at a conference are each born on one of the seven days of the week.
Dividing 100 by 7 gives about 14.
3, so at least one weekday is the birthday of 15 or more of them.
The rule is to divide the number of items by the number of boxes and round up.
With 10 pigeons and 3 holes, some hole has at least 4.
This is how you can prove that among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month, and among any 25, at least three were.
The handshake puzzle.
At a party, guests shake hands with some others, never with themselves or twice with the same person.
Prove that two guests shook exactly the same number of hands.
Say there are 20 guests.
Each person's count could be anything from 0 to 19, which looks like 20 values for 20 people, just enough to all differ.
But look closer.
If someone shook nobody's hand, then nobody can have shaken all 19 others.
So 0 and 19 cannot both appear.
That leaves only 19 usable holes for 20 guests, and two people must share a count.
The trick is common: first show there are fewer real options than there seem.
Limits and habits of mind.
The principle sets hard limits in computing.
Could a clever program shrink every possible file, even by one bit?
Counting says no.
There are 1,024 different files exactly 10 bits long but only 1,023 shorter ones, including the empty file.
If every 10-bit file shrank, two would share a compressed version and the program could not know which to restore.
Real compression works because everyday files are full of patterns; truly random data cannot be squeezed.
The same logic explains why hash functions, which turn any data into a short fingerprint, must sometimes give two inputs the same fingerprint.
Security depends on making such collisions extraordinarily hard to find.
The principle guarantees only that a match exists, not where it is.
The key idea: If more items go into fewer boxes, some box must hold two, which proves something exists without finding it.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why does the chessboard reward grow so enormous?
Answer. Each square doubles the one before, so totals explode late.
Question two. What is a year's ‘doomsday’?
Answer. The weekday shared by 4/4, 6/6 and 8/8.
Question three. Why does switching doors win two thirds of the time?
Answer. Your first pick is usually wrong, so the other door usually wins.
Question four. What can the pigeonhole principle prove?
Answer. That some box must be shared.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
